newsitem.title: UK: Conventional ads seen doomed to fail on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Conventional ads seen doomed to fail on Internet.

text.p: An advertising executive warned colleagues on Thursday against putting conventional advertising on the Internet and said on-line consumers wanted information and other "freebies" -- not a hard sell.

Sheila Byfield, media development director at Network Europe, which is owned by WPP Group Plc, told a business conference that advertisers also had to take into account consumers' growing sceptism about advertising.

"It is clear that conventional set piece advertising -- effectively a miniature TV programme -- has no real place in future media such as infomercials, interactive ads intended for on-line interactive services and teletext style text ads," she said.
Byfield said Network Europe -- which is part of ad agency Ogilvy & Mather -- has been researching how consumer attitudes to the media will evolve in the future.
Network Europe is working on the research project, which is called futura.com, with the Independent Television Commission, which regulates commercial TV in Britain, and the University of Leeds.
Byfield said initial findings indicated consumers wanted information from commercial messages on new media such as the Internet, rather than conventional "hard sell" advertising.

"Most people are somewhat cynical about advertising and marketing and are aware that, ultimately, the only reason that companies will offer electronic facilities is because they see it as a way of increasing profits. Consumers are asking, 'What's in it for me?' They are suspicious of being sold at," she said.

But Byfield said told the second Media International Objective Research Conference there was a trade-off and that consumers would look at ads on the Internet, for example, if they got something out of it.
She cited an animated screensaver for Guinness Plc which Internet users could download for free last year as a successful example.

Advertising that interrupts a consumer's activity, such as full page on-line ads or those introduced by a Swedish telephone company that offered cheap calls to phone users prepared to have conversations interrupted by ads, can provoke very negative reactions, she said.
